extracted.intended_audience: readers/students of moral and political philosophy; scholars of ethics and legal theory
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic exposition of the concepts of wrong, right, property, contract, the origin and purpose of the state, and the moral justification and limits of punishment. The text sets out principled criteria for when actions are wrong or right and how political institutions should be justified by moral theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Wrong
rubrics_metrics.description: Wrong is the quality of conduct in which an individual extends the assertion of the will appearing in his own body so far that it becomes the denial of the will appearing in the bodies of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes gradations from the highest (cannibalism) to murder, mutilation/injury, subjugation/slavery, and seizure of another’s goods; the text explains wrong as denial of another’s assertion of will and illustrates with concrete examples (murder → immediate remorse; seizure of goods equated with making someone a slave).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral basis of property: labour as foundation
rubrics_metrics.description: True (moral) right of property is based simply and solely on work expended by a person on a thing; property not taken from a man without wrong can only be that which has been produced by his own powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and contrasts: quoting Laws of Manu; rejection of Kant’s first-occupation theory as insufficient; mere past enjoyment or mere avowal/desire for sole possession gives no moral right; improvement, cultivation, preservation (even slight labour like picking fruit) grounds ownership; land/hunting enjoyed without improvement cannot morally exclude newcomers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wrong can arise by violence or by craft (equally morally essential)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wrong generally occurs either through violence (physical causality) or through craft (motivation/causality via knowledge); morally it matters not which path is used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violence achieves domination by physical force; craft achieves it by falsifying knowledge (lies) that motivate another’s will. Both result in compelling another to serve the actor’s will instead of his own.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and moral status of the Lie
rubrics_metrics.description: A lie always aims at influencing another’s will by falsifying his knowledge; every imposing of a lie is a wrong because it extends the authority of my will over another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes mere refusal to assert a truth (not itself wrong) from active deception (wrong). Examples: directing a traveller to a false road is wrong; boastful conduct and lies for self-interest or wickedness are covered. The most complete lie is the broken contract (see separate criterion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Broken contract as the most complete lie and moral wrong
rubrics_metrics.description: The broken contract is the most complete lie because promises were exchanged as mutual motives, and breaking the covenant deceives by introducing illusory motives into another’s knowledge and bending his will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why promises exchanged with assumed power to perform ground mutual performance; breaking the promise constitutes distinct wrong and is the moral basis for the lawfulness and validity of contract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shamefulness: craft more shameful than violence
rubrics_metrics.description: Wrong through craft (deception, faithlessness, treachery) is more shameful than wrong through violence because it betrays weakness and breaks the bond of good faith that unites individuals externally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues craft lowers man morally and physically and excites deep horror because good faith externally binds disparate wills into unity; faithlessness expands the consequences of egoism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right defined negatively as the negation of wrong
rubrics_metrics.description: The concept of right is derivative and negative — it contains merely the negation of wrong; actions are right insofar as they do not transgress the limit of denying another’s will for the stronger assertion of one’s own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implications: refusal of help, or cold inaction (contemplating another’s suffering while having more than enough) may be cruel but is not, strictly speaking, 'wrong' by this moral definition. The boundary between right and wrong divides possible actions morally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of compulsion / self-defence (warding off wrong)
rubrics_metrics.description: Warding off an attempted wrong cannot itself be wrong; one has a right to deny that denial of another by the force necessary to overcome it — this can extend to killing when necessary to ward off an encroachment on the will embodied in one’s person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains this as negation of the negation: my defensive action affirms my own embodied will and does not encroach on another’s. Examples include killing in self-defence when another’s external violence threatens the assertion of one’s body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to use craft where right of compulsion exists (permissible deception in defence)
rubrics_metrics.description: One has an actual right to lie precisely insofar as one has a right of compulsion; deception used to defend oneself or recover what is rightly one’s own is permissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: assuring a highway robber you have nothing on you; tricking a burglar into a cellar and locking him; a captive deceiving robbers to regain freedom; using false dice against someone who plays with money stolen from you; stratagems in war as acted lies are justified. The text contrasts moral unlawfulness of lies generally with permissibility in defensive contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics concerns action/will; politics concerns suffering/outward effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethics (pure doctrine of right) treats the will and action as the object (inner significance); the state/politics is exclusively concerned with the suffering of wrong (outward events) and with preventing suffering by making the deed the focus of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: state does not aim to eradicate inward disposition but aims to place counter-motives (punishments) beside motives for wrong; criminal code catalogs motives to deter conduct. Ethics provides limits between right and wrong which legislation inverts and applies from the passive (sufferer) side.

rubrics_metrics.name: State as contract to renounce inflicting wrong to reduce suffering
rubrics_metrics.description: The state originates as a contract whereby individuals renounce inflicting wrong to diminish the general suffering caused by mutual egoism; it is formed by reasoned self-interest to secure mutual wellbeing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The account aligns with Plato and Hobbes: the state arises to reduce overall suffering and divide it more equally; forms of state (republic, monarchy, etc.) vary in perfection depending on freedom from anarchy/despotism; the state serves egoism methodically, not as a promoter of inward morality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of the state: only negative duties enforceable by force
rubrics_metrics.description: The state can enforce only negative duties (rights) by force; it cannot compel benevolence or exact obligations of love (positive duties) because these require someone to assume the active role no one will willingly take without moral motive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus legislation criminalizes acts to prevent suffering of wrong but cannot make people genuinely benevolent; the state’s end is well-being (salus publica) rather than inner moral transformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive law as basis of right to punish; punishment’s end is deterrence, not revenge
rubrics_metrics.description: All right to punish is based on positive law that pre-defines punishments before offences; the immediate end of punishment is the fulfilment of the law as a contract and chiefly deterrence of future infringements — punishment is forward-looking, not retributive revenge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes punishment from revenge: revenge aims at past consolation, has no moral justification. Kantian retributive formulations (jus talionis, expiation) are rejected as groundless. Punishment must be announced as inevitable for deterrence to work; example of English indictment language emphasises deterrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kantian critique: state is not the moral condition for freedom nor does punishment justify treating people as means without qualification
rubrics_metrics.description: The text rejects Kant’s claims that the state is an institution for furthering morality or that punishment as mere requital is justified; while punishment may 'use' a criminal as a means to public security, this is justified by the state’s end (public safety) and by pre-established law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues the Kantian maxim 'Man must always be treated as an end, never as a means' is vague and requires specification; using a condemned murderer as means to restore security is morally justified under the deterrence/fulfilment-of-contract view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper relation between pure (moral) theory of right and positive legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: Positive legislation is the inverted application of the pure moral doctrine of right; only if positive law is in essential matters grounded in the pure theory of right does it constitute a state 'based upon right' and morally permissible — otherwise it is a positive wrong (despotism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists principal points the pure doctrine must provide for legislation: (1) explanation of inner significance of wrong/right; (2) deduction of law of property; (3) deduction of moral validity of contracts; (4) explanation of origin/aim of the state and inversion to legislation; (5) deduction of right of punishment. If legislation cannot be grounded in these, institutions like serfdom or vassalage are unjust.
